item.title: GOP's losses will raise pressure on conservative Supreme Court justices to retire
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The GOP’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections Tuesday set up an unsettling possibility for the party: If it doesn’t act now to confirm a new Supreme Court justice, it may not have another chance for years to come. That prospect is likely to ramp up pressure on the court’s two oldest conservatives - Justices Samuel A. Alito Jr., 76, and Clarence Thomas, 78 - to retire during the lame-duck period, while Republicans still have the votes to get a nominee confirmed by the Senate. The new Senate, in which Democrats will hold a majority, is seated on Jan. 3. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Alito, who joined the court in 2006, said last month he has no plans to retire during the lame-duck session. Thomas has said in the past he has no plans to step down from the court. He joined the court in 1991 and could become the longest-serving justice in its history in 2028. But given the magnitude of Democratic inroads in the Senate, legal and political experts said it could be 2033 before Republicans have a realistic shot at winning back enough seats in that chamber to approve a conservative justice. At that point, Alito and Thomas would be well into their 80s. Neither responded to a request for comment. “I think both have been making an implicit bet that they will live long enough … so that a Republican president can replace them with someone ideologically similar,” said Ed Whelan, a conservative attorney and senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center. This is likely to make many Republicans antsy, particularly those mindful of the lesson of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who died while still on the bench at 87, in September 2020. The liberal justice’s death allowed Republicans to move the court in a more conservative direction when they confirmed Justice Amy Coney Barrett to replace her weeks later. President Donald Trump nominated Barrett to replace Ginsburg, and over the vociferous objections of Democrats, Senate Republicans quickly muscled the nomination through just ahead of the 2020 presidential election. Trump remade the court with three picks in his first term - Barrett, Neil M. Gorsuch and Brett M. Kavanaugh - who pushed the court sharply to the right. The Supreme Court’s conservative 6-3 supermajority has delivered historic opinions on abortion, affirmative action, religious rights and much more that have thrilled Republicans. A younger replacement for Alito or Thomas could lock that advantage in for years to come. Liberals accused Republicans of hypocrisy for rapidly confirming Barrett after they blocked President Barack Obama’s nomination of Merrick Garland for 11 months in 2016, saying it was too close to the presidential election to confirm him. Trump won the White House, and Garland’s nomination was scuttled. Some observers think the window has already closed for Trump to nominate a fourth justice, which would allow him to leave a mark on the Supreme Court that few presidents have enjoyed. Republicans control 53 seats in the upper chamber, compared with 47 held by Democrats. But that split will shift to 52-48 as soon as Dec. 15, when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is seated as a result of a special election. A handful of moderate Senate Republicans like Maine’s Susan Collins and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski might also have to be persuaded to back a Trump pick. The margin of error is thin enough that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) posted Tuesday night on X that Trump probably won’t be able to get a suitable nominee confirmed. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump’s term: Zero,” DeSantis wrote. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won’t be able to recapture enough seats in 28).” Harry Litman, a law professor at UCLA and a former U.S. attorney, said the optics of a justice retiring during the lame-duck session would also tarnish his or her reputation. “It would be the most crass and nakedly political resignation in the court’s history,” Litman said. Emily Hampsten, a spokeswoman for Sen. Dick Durbin (Illinois), the Democratic whip and a member of the Judiciary Committee, said a lame-duck nominee would create a backlash among voters and Democrats. “The American people will hold them accountable in 2028, and Democrats could justifiably refuse to confirm any Trump nominees for the next two years,” Hampsten said. That would curtail one of Trump’s other biggest legacies - the nomination of hundreds of lower court federal judges. Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown law professor, wrote on his blog that a lame-duck confirmation fight might also backfire on the GOP by building support for court reforms that Democrats are already eyeing during the next Congress. “The question would no longer be whether the Court deserves to be restructured, but whether the other side has left Democrats any choice,” Vladeck wrote. Gabe Roth, executive director of the reform group Fix the Court, said he thinks only small reforms will be possible while Trump is still president over the next two years. “Democrats would do well to focus on areas within the realm of court reform where there’s already strong bipartisan support,” Roth said. “That includes banning stock trading in the federal courts, adding more lower court judgeships to relieve ballooning caseloads, improving workplace conduct protections for judiciary staff and making access to court records free.” Speculation over whether Alito would retire flared over the summer when NPR published an erroneous account saying he was planning on stepping down. The story was later retracted. Alito said during a round of interviews to promote his new book last month that he had no plans to retire during the current term, which will end in June or July. The justice said he has more to contribute to the court but did consider whether to continue each term. “I intend to stick around through this term,” Alito said in the interview before the Supreme Court’s new term began last month. “I made that decision many months ago.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/05/gops-losses-will-raise-pressure-conservative-supreme-court-justices-retire/

item.title: New DNA technology could solve JonBenét Ramsey's killing 30 years later
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In the early hours of Dec. 26, 1996, after a festive family Christmas, Patsy Ramsey walked down the stairs in her Boulder, Colorado, home to discover a terrifying ransom note telling her that her 6-year-old daughter JonBenét Ramsey had been kidnapped. She immediately called 911 and the Boulder Police Department responded to the scene in three minutes. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: JonBenét Ramsey was 6 years old when she was found dead in her home in Boulder, Co. on Dec. 26, 1996. The taunting two-and-a-half-page ransom note was addressed to JonBenét's father, John Ramsey, and demanded $118,000 for the safe return of his daughter. "You stand a 99% chance of killing your daughter if you try to out smart [sic] us," the letter said. There was no sign of JonBenét or further communication from the would-be kidnappers. A new "20/20" episode, "JonBenét R a msey: R a ce Against Time, Who is 'Unknown Male 1?' -- A New Diane Sawyer Investigation" ai r ing F r iday, Nov. 6 at 9 p.m. ET on ABC and st r eaming the next day on Disney+ and H u l u , re-examines the case. Yo u can get mo r e behind the scenes of each week's episode by listening to "20/20: The Afte r Show" weekly se r ies r ight on yo u r 20/20 podcast feed on Mondays, hosted by "20/20" co-ancho r Debo r a h R obe r ts. Hours later, a police officer asked John Ramsey and a friend to look through the house to see if anything seemed out of place. John Ramsey discovered his daughter’s lifeless body in the basement of their home. DNA testing confirms 'serial killer' in Pennsylvania in 1970s: State police An autopsy report determined that JonBenét had been sexually assaulted and killed by blunt force trauma to the head and strangulation, which was carried out with a makeshift corded torture device called a garrote. With 19 new interviews, ABC News anchor Diane Sawyer and chief investigative correspondent Aaron Katersky take a fresh look at this cold case, talking with investigators, forensic scientists, genealogy experts, the Boulder Police chief and JonBenét's brothers Burke Ramsey and John Andrew Ramsey, among others. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: JonBenét Ramsey with her mother, Patsy Ramsey, both of whom competed in pageants. In the weeks and months after the murder, members of the Ramsey family came under intense scrutiny by both the Boulder police and the general public. Skeptics of the family pointed to several details of the case, including the ransom note, which some close to the investigation believed was staged by a family member to cover up JonBenét's death. The note was written on Patsy Ramsey’s notepad but after numerous handwriting comparisons, only one indicated that the samples showed any similarities to Patsy’s writing. The Ramsey family vehemently denied any claims they were involved in their daughter's death. In 2008, DNA was detected on the outside of JonBenét's pajama bottoms using a new testing method called touch DNA analysis. It matched the DNA found inside JonBenét's underwear and traced to the same unknown male, and not to any member of the Ramsey family. ABC News - PHOTO: ABC News anchor Diane Sawyer and chief investigative correspondent Aaron Katersky reinvestigated JonBenét Ramsey's case with new interviews. Nancy Guthrie abduction: FBI analyzing DNA recovered from her home, sources say With this development, then-Boulder County District Attorney Mary Lacy wrote a letter to John Ramsey. "This new scientific evidence convinces us that it is appropriate, given the circumstances of this case, to state that we do not consider your immediate family, including you, your wife, Patsy, and your son, Burke, to be under any suspicion in the commission of this crime," Lacy wrote. "I wish we could have done so before Mrs. Ramsey died." Patsy Ramsey died from ovarian cancer in 2006 , two years before Mary Lacy’s letter to the family. Later, some Boulder officials said Lacy's letter was inappropriate for a prosecutor, and she should not have cleared the Ramseys while the investigation was ongoing. In recent years, a new technology called single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) has made it possible to solve cold murder cases nationwide . The advanced testing can retrieve DNA from miniscule samples. Combined with genetic genealogy, it allows officials to identify suspects by matching DNA to that of distant family members in law enforcement databases, using online genetic databases. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: The Ramsey family has searched for JonBenét Ramsey's murderer for 30 years. How a man murdered his estranged wife and fled state with teen girlfriend Even with this promising new development, challenges remain for investigators. Some DNA samples obtained from the body and crime scene are very small and complex, as multiple DNA strands are mixed together, making it difficult to verifiably match with a single individual. The current Boulder Police Chief Stephen Redfearn had never before done an interview about the Ramsey case. He sat down with ABC News' Sawyer, telling her that his department is in talks with labs that might be able to test the DNA using forensic genetic genealogy. JonBenét Ramsey's father says advances in DNA technology can help police solve daughter's 1996 murder He said they are hesitant to send any sample until they have full confidence that the technology is advanced enough to get results that help progress the case. In some cases, if the sample is very small, it can be consumed by the testing. "We might get lucky because we may only, in some circumstances, with what we have, have one shot at getting it tested," Redfearn said. Redfearn said they are re-interviewing suspects, testing new evidence and pursuing every lead. "I would love nothing more than 30 years since this little girl was murdered in her own home, someone finally decides to get something off their chest," he said. JonBenét Ramsey case gets renewed attention ABC News - PHOTO: Burke Ramsey, JonBenét's brother, gave an exclusive interview after largely staying out of the public eye since his sister's murder. Burke Ramsey, who has largely stayed out of the public eye since his sister's death, praised his parents for how strong they were in the aftermath of the tragedy. "This awful thing happened to this family, and the world turns against you. And it's cruel," he said. ABC News - PHOTO: John Andrew Ramsey, JonBenét Ramsey's half brother, has sought justice for his half sister's murder for three decades. JonBenét’s older half-brother, John Andrew Ramsey, said investigators must have courage and act aggressively to get the case solved as soon as possible. "I know we're going to find this person," he said. "This is a case that can be solved. There's a mountain of evidence out there. We've got the DNA testing that's in our favor. It's not a question of if, but when." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/new-dna-tech-solve-jonbent-ramseys-murder-case/story?id=137603999

item.title: Vance faces a 2028 dilemma as Republicans question his ties to Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP's devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions. The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance. It’s a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large. “The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance’s 2028 prospects,” said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. “Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30’s and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question,” Madden added. Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger. “Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing,” said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis. “This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win,” the operative added. In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war. “Vance’s profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle,” Madden predicted. The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 “is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren’t substantial changes.” If there aren’t changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president. DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind. The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices. In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of “gaslighting” voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety. DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That’s an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state. Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion. Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms. On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP’s terrible night. He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs. “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” he said. GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday’s results, their primary will be wide open. “Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday,” one former Trump campaign aide said. “It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance.” Other Republicans say Tuesday’s results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field. “Vance needs to announce first with the president’s endorsement,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “If he doesn’t do it in January, it’ll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn’t on board. And that’s the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?” One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there’s “more space than less space” for other Republicans to enter the race. “Let’s face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night,” the former aide said. “This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era." The former aide added that Trump “is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that’s 30 percent right off the bat." But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances. “Imagine, he’s going to have to answer to Trump’s whim or rant of the day every day,” the former aide said. “And he’s not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him. “That’s just not an enviable place,” the former aide added. Since the elections, Vance has been under scrutiny from both Republicans and Democrats. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who served under former President George W. Bush, took to social platform X to counter Vance’s evaluation of the sweeping GOP losses. “Please allow me to present a different perspective,” Fleischer said. “The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire. If you start a war, you need to win it and finish it - otherwise don’t start it.” Democrats also pounced on Vance’s remarks. “For you to reduce it to a simple political calculation while we still have 50,000 troops in the Middle East, is one of the most crass, cynical things I’ve seen,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), wrote Wednesday on X. “You and President Trump got us into this war without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It’s cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure with no end in sight.” On Thursday, as political pundits were saying it was the end of the Trump era, Republicans said Vance’s political future remained murky at best. “I think if you’re Vance you gotta take the nomination and pray you get someone on the other side like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez,” the first former Trump aide said, referring to the progressive representative from New York. For now, Del Percio said, results aside, Vance “ultimately stands in the same place he did three weeks ago.” “He only exists at the whim of the president,” she said. “And if Trump doesn’t endorse, will Vance go without the president’s endorsement? If he’s forced to do that, he will break with Trump and it will get ugly.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Meghan Markle's father Thomas arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges related to child sexual abuse material, authorities said. Markle, 82, was arrested by the FBI at a care home near Tampa, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said in a press release . He was charged with one count of possession of child pornography. Authorities said Markle was arrested after agents discovered approximately 78 items — including slides, film negatives, and books — that contained suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) while searching two storage units registered to Markle, at least one of which was in the Los Angeles area. "Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law." The statement said that, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding the discovery of suspected CSAM among Markle's possessions in the Philippines. Officers then interviewed a separate individual who revealed Markle had rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. This led to the discovery of a second storage unit. Both had been rented by Markle since 2008. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that “Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions.” “This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide,” Patel added. If convicted, Markle would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. He is expected to appear in court in Tampa on Friday. "This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," said Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office. In October, it was reported that Markle was under investigation in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. He has not been charged by police in the Philippines. The Sun first reported that his son, Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., told Philippine police that after his father left the country in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu. Markle Sr. denied those allegations, telling the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick." Markle is believed to have returned to the U.S. in May, after his left leg was amputated in the Philippines in December 2025. In October, The Sun reported Markle moved into Maravida Senior Living care home, a facility which specializes in "memory care." Meghan Markle released a statement following the claims, saying she was "deeply distressed." She also revealed that in 2019 she received a copy of a letter containing "troubling" allegations about him, which had been sent to London's Metropolitan Police. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police subsequently said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies. According to the Sun on Sunday , Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case. Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them." She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/thomas-markle-arrested-by-fbi-on-charges-linked-to-child-sexual-abuse-material-reports-say-153545681.html

item.title: Trump replaces Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats continue to celebrate one of the most lopsided midterm election victories in modern U.S. history, routing their Republican rivals to gain control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and now hold 54 to the Republican Party's 44. Two seats — nail-biting contests in Alaska and Mississippi — remain undeclared. In the House, Democrats held 253 House seats to the GOP's 161 as of 2 p.m. ET Friday, comfortably passing the majority threshold of 218, with 21 races yet to be called. The latest estimates show that the party is on track to win its largest majority since 2008. And there are still seats it could flip, including Colorado's Fourth District, which is held by Republican incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert, a staunch Trump ally, whose race against Democrat Eileen Laubacher remains tight. There were also gubernatorial races , mayoral contests, ballot measures — and plenty of firsts. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect. El-Sayed will be America's first Muslim senator. In a big post-election shake-up, President Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, a top deputy widely viewed as one of the most influential figures behind the administration's agenda, is replacing Susie Wiles as his chief of staff. Earlier this week, Trump signaled he would work with Democrats during his remaining two years in office but said he wouldn't hesitate to use his veto power. Trump also acknowledged that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses, but defended his decision to pursue the conflict. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said, adding: "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Vice President JD Vance, though, blamed the scale of GOP losses squarely on the war with Iran. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," he wrote in a post on X . "The reason we lost is the war." item.title: 2 DOJ officials resign, including attorney who oversaw 'grand conspiracy' probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday. Jason Reding Quiñones' resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues. The Justice Department's top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department's Civil Rights Division , also announced her departure. Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president. His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones' "leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro." Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones' office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with "immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation." "I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law," Quiñones wrote in a social media post. The "grand conspiracy" investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case. Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges. Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department's National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters. Among the division's most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing. "He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation's ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic," Blanche said in a statement. item.title: Data centers get blamed for soaring electric bills. A new study points elsewhere.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On Tuesday, Americans voted overwhelmingly against data centers and artificial intelligence growth. In 40 of 41 local ballot races around the country, many in the state of Ohio, voters opted to restrict or prohibit new data center constructions in their areas. Much of the growing opposition to data centers has come from rising electricity prices , which are squeezing Americans in a time of already high prices and cost of living. But, according to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices. The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4 percent of the utility rate increases over the last five years. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free “Even to me it was somewhat surprising,” said Serguei Netessine, professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and one of the study’s authors. In the run-up to the elections, Democrats pointed to data centers — and Republican support for their development — as key drivers of electricity price increases. In one campaign ad , Democrat James Talarico, now senator-elect of Texas, said that Texans were “paying the price with skyrocketing utility bills.” Sherrod Brown, Democratic senator-elect of Ohio, similarly argued that state residents were facing higher electricity bills due to the build-out of energy-hogging data centers. There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1 percent. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices. Most Read From The Washington Post Sullivan and Peltola remain neck-and-neck in Alaska Senate race Colom’s lead grows over Hyde-Smith in Mississippi race amid legal saber-rattling Hegseth not under consideration to be appointed to Senate Judge halts Trump’s arch after federal panel approves it Republicans in North Carolina lose 4 more House seats as GOP wipeout spreads “Depending on which techniques you use, you can identify a slight increase or decrease in prices historically” due to data centers, said Ryan Hledik, principal at the Brattle Group. “None of these are the kind of earth-shattering rate impacts you hear about.” The new Harvard and Penn study found a slightly higher impact on industrial electricity prices — the price paid by manufacturers and large facilities. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15 percent of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans, Netessine said, the changes simply were not substantial. “So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much,” Netessine said. Instead, he said, prices are rising due to more quotidian factors: rising gas prices, an aging electricity grid, and wildfires and hurricanes requiring improvements to the grid and recovery after disaster. Most of the cost of generating and delivering electricity is based on large, up-front capital costs, such as the costs to build power plants, wires and transmission lines to carry that power into homes. Some areas of the United States also have excess “capacity” in the grid — meaning that the grid is overbuilt for the actual demand. In those areas, adding a data center means that large fixed grid costs are spread over more consumers. That could lower prices. Of course, that’s not the case everywhere. PJM has had booming data center growth that has also required additional build-out of the power grid. This has raised prices at power capacity auctions, and states like Maryland have seen increasing residential prices that are at least in part from this boom. If the number of data centers continue to boom, experts say, residential prices could be affected more down the line. Data center electricity demand is expected to increase steeply over the next few years, requiring new power generation — wind, solar or natural gas — to be put onto the grid. And residents have issues with data centers that go beyond the price of electricity. The new developments have been singled out for loud noise , polluting power generation , and for disturbing residential neighborhoods and natural landscapes. According to the Pew Research Center, more than half of Americans say that data centers are mostly bad for the environment. Others feel that the AI race — which could ultimately leave many Americans out of work — is being forced upon them. “I think generally what we’re seeing is a broader range of reasons the public has opposed data centers,” Hledik said. “Concern about AI leading to loss of jobs — all of that is getting packaged together.” This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/06/data-centers-may-not-be-raising-americans-electricity-bills-that-much/

item.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
So long, Tesla ( TSLA ) Cybertruck, we hardly knew ye. Yes, it is official. The Tesla Cybertruck will soon be no more, per a post from CEO Elon Musk on his X account. "Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote early Friday morning. For many in the industry, this isn't a surprise even with Musk's grand pronouncements about the vehicle. Musk once boasted that Cybertruck demand was " so far off the hook, you can't even see the hook ," and the company said it had over 1 million preorders. Tesla CEO Elon Musk introduces the Cybertruck at Tesla's design studio in Hawthorne, Calif on Thursday, Nov. 21, 2019. (AP Photo/Ringo H.W. Chiu, File) ASSOCIATED PRESS But conversion to sales never materialized. Cox Automotive's Kelley Blue Book estimated overall sales for the controversial pickup only hit around 71,000 since the vehicle went on sale in 2023. Tesla and Musk had built out capacity for Giga Austin to pump out 250K Cybertrucks per year; Tesla was selling about one-tenth that amount. When the truck was first revealed in late 2019 , Musk had promised a sub-$40,000 price tag for the cheapest version, and up to 500 miles of range for the top-end model. None of these things materialized. Tesla had wanted to get the first models out by late 2021, but delays in finalizing design, creating the large stainless steel body panels, and, of course, the pandemic delayed its release. Now, after a near four-year run (by mid 2027), the Cybertruck is no more. Musk and Tesla point to the need to boost production of the upcoming Cybercab, which has been testing in certain robotaxi markets. The Cybercab — which has no steering wheel or pedals — is a huge bet on autonomy and essentially ride-sharing as opposed to private ownership (though Tesla says the Cybercab will eventually go on sale to consumers). The Cybertruck's discontinuation comes after the cancellation of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV, two of Tesla's most significant — though pricey — models. At the time, Musk said the space at its Fremont factory where the S and X were made was needed for Optimus robot lines. Now the EV truck space has a bit more clarity. Rivian's R1T pickup and GM’s Chevrolet Silverado/GMC Sierra EV are now the only options; however, Ford will soon release the Fathom compact EV pickup . Then there's Slate , the startup with a no-frills, bare-bones $25K pickup. Musk's soaring vision of Tesla as a robotics, software, and autonomy company is becoming clear. But many Tesla fans who enjoy driving their own vehicles may be concerned about what happens to the company's remaining EVs for sale — if the bet for Tesla is on tech rather than cars. Pras Subramanian is the lead auto reporter for Yahoo Finance. You can follow him on X and on Instagram . item.title: Sen. Chris Murphy is released from hospital after hemorrhagic stroke
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut was released from the hospital Friday after experiencing a stroke nearly a week ago, but will miss several weeks of votes as he continues his recovery at a rehabilitation center. "I want to be direct with you, so here is my diagnosis," Murphy said in a statement. "Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 9-1-1 out of an abundance of caution, and I'm glad I did." Murphy, who is 53, said he was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of his brain. The thalamus sits above the brainstem and relays sensory information between the spinal cord and the brain, according to the Cleveland Clinic . Dr. Jose Suarez, the chief of neurosciences critical care at Johns Hopkins, where Murphy was hospitalized, said the senator experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke. "He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation," Suarez said in a statement released by Murphy's office. Murphy said he is taking his recovery seriously and will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center in order to "get back to work on the quickest timeline possible." "This has been a scary experience for me and my family, and I appreciate the continued respect for our privacy," Murphy said. "As I'm working towards a full recovery, I am staying engaged with my team and colleagues remotely, and my staff continues to carry out our legislative priorities, serve constituents, and ensure the work of my office continues uninterrupted." Murphy's office announced Sunday that he had numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game and was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered that he had a stroke. He was then transferred to Johns Hopkins. The senator has been viewed as a possible contender for the White House in 2028.
